resources.string: Takakia
Takakia ceratophylla
Takakia moss

A minute bryophyte with branched leafy shoots pressed against the substrate. Its deeply lobed leaves distinguish it from many mosses. Sporophytes are rare; the plant is mainly recognized by its vegetative form and unusual phylogenetic position.
Cool, wet high mountains of East Asia; also recorded in north-western North America.
Creeping or ascending shoots only millimetres tall, anchored by rhizoids.
Narrow leaves deeply split into lobes and arranged spirally.
No flowers: mosses bear reproductive organs on the gametophyte and reproduce by spores.
Rare spore capsule on a very short sporophyte.
Hair-cap moss
Polytrichum piliferum
white hair-point moss

A low cushion-forming moss, notable for the long white hyaline hairpoint that often extends from each leaf. It colonizes open, nutrient-poor surfaces; reddish-brown capsules may occur on an upright seta.
Temperate and boreal regions, especially exposed acidic, sandy or rocky soils.
Low dense tufts that may look silvery because of their pale leaf tips.
Narrow leaves ending in a long white hyaline hairpoint; margins ciliate.
No flowers; reproductive organs are borne at the shoot tips.
Angular reddish-brown capsule, sometimes with a hairy calyptra; sporophytes are often absent.
Floating crystalwort
Riccia fluitans
floating Riccia

An aquatic liverwort without true stems or leaves: its gametophyte forms green ribbons that branch dichotomously and float as mats. Submerged and terrestrial forms differ; sporophytes are rarely visible in floating populations.
Shallow still waters, ditches and ponds in temperate and tropical regions; also grown in aquaria.
Floating thallus of forked ribbons, often tangled into a surface mat.
No true leaves: flattened thallus ribbons bear rhizoids underneath.
No flowers; spores develop in sporophytes embedded in the thallus.
Inconspicuous capsule, usually invisible without close examination.
Springy turf-moss
Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus
yard moss
A pleurocarpous moss forming loose mats with prostrate stems and spreading branches. Its useful character is the squarrose leaf posture: leaves project sharply outward and curve away from the stem.
Cool temperate regions; lawns, meadows and damp grassy places.
Loose mats with creeping stems and irregular branching.
Small narrow leaves abruptly reflected from the stem; a single costa.
No flowers; capsules are borne on sporophytes, which are often uncommon.
Ovoid capsule inclined to horizontal on a slender seta; it may be absent.
Papuan cedar
Papuacedrus papuana
Papua cedar
An evergreen conifer that can become a large tree, with fibrous bark and flattened fan-like sprays. Opposite scale leaves occur in two forms on adult shoots; small woody cones bear winged seeds.
Native from the Moluccas to New Guinea, mainly in montane forests.
Conical tree with tiered branches and flattened sprays; bark becomes fibrous with age.
Opposite dimorphic scale leaves on flattened shoots.
No flowers; male and female cones are separate.
Small woody female cones; seeds have unequal wings.
Guaitecas cypress
Pilgerodendron uviferum
Chilean cypress

A conifer of the cold, very wet forests of southern South America. It bears opposite scale foliage on flattened shoots and very small globose cones; its habit ranges from a gnarled shrub to a slender tree.
Southern Chile and Argentina, in Patagonian rainforest and peatlands.
Evergreen tree with a narrow, often irregular outline in exposed peatlands.
Small scale leaves in opposite pairs, decurrent along the shoots.
No flowers; pollen and ovules occur on separate cones.
Nearly spherical female cone made of a few woody scales.
Pancher’s neocallitropsis
Neocallitropsis pancheri
Callitris pancheri, name accepted by Kew
A New Caledonian conifer of maquis and forests on ultramafic substrates. POWO treats Neocallitropsis pancheri as a synonym of Callitris pancheri; this profile retains the tree terminal’s name.
Endemic to New Caledonia; associated with metal-rich ultramafic ground.
Evergreen shrub or small tree with scale-clad short shoots.
Minute imbricate scale leaves in tight whorls.
No flowers; male and female conifer cones.
Globose woody female cones release winged seeds.
Chinese white-berry yew
Pseudotaxus chienii
white-berried yew
A small evergreen dioecious tree or shrub endemic to China. Its flat needles have two pale stomatal bands beneath; the single seed is surrounded by a white aril, unlike yews with red arils.
Forests and rocky slopes of south-eastern China.
Spreading shrub or small tree, often on rocky slopes.
Flattened needles in two ranks, with two whitish bands underneath.
No flowers; male and female reproductive structures occur on separate plants.
Single seed partly enclosed by a fleshy white aril; it is not a berry.
Puerto Rico royal palm
Roystonea borinquena
Puerto Rican royal palm

A tall solitary palm with a smooth pale-grey trunk and a crown of long pinnate leaves. The green shaft below the crown is formed by leaf sheaths. Roystonea species identification also relies on provenance and finer characters.
Native to Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands in humid tropical habitats.
Single straight grey trunk with a green crownshaft below the crown.
Very large pinnate leaves with numerous linear leaflets.
Branched inflorescences emerge below the crownshaft; flowers are small and unisexual.
Small ovoid drupes, green then purple-black when mature.
Stilt-root palm
Iriartea deltoidea
Iriartea palm

A Neotropical palm recognizable by its cluster of spiny stilt roots around the trunk. Large pinnate leaves bear leaflets often grouped and oriented in several planes, giving an irregular feathered appearance.
Humid forests from Central America to western Amazonia.
Solitary trunk supported by aerial stilt roots, sometimes spiny.
Long pinnate leaves with grouped leaflets, sometimes arranged in several planes.
Branched inflorescences below the leaves bear small male and female flowers.
Small ovoid to ellipsoid drupes, green then dark.
Tagua palm
Ammandra decasperma
ten-seeded palm

A palm with almost no visible trunk, bearing huge pinnate leaves that emerge from the ground. Fruits cluster near the base; their hard seeds have been worked as vegetable ivory. Ecological data are limited.
North-western Colombia and Ecuador, in lowland rainforest.
Acaulescent or subterranean-trunk palm with arching leaves and ground-level fruits.
Very long pinnate leaves with numerous leaflets.
Inflorescences near the ground beneath the leaves; flowers small and unisexual.
Large fruits contain a few hard seeds with white endosperm, used as vegetable ivory.
Strict primrose
Primula stricta
Arctic primrose
A small perennial primrose with a narrow basal rosette and leafless scapes. Lilac to violet flowers have a yellow throat and cluster at the scape tip; the capsule opens by valves at maturity.
Arctic and subarctic Europe and North America, in open wet habitats.
Low rosette producing a slender flower stalk taller than the leaves.
Narrow basal leaves, nearly linear to spatulate, entire or weakly toothed.
Umbel of five-lobed lilac-violet flowers with a yellow throat.
Ovoid capsule opening by valves and releasing numerous seeds.
Japanese sacred lily
Rohdea japonica
Japanese rohdea

An evergreen rhizomatous perennial forming a dense rosette of leathery strap-shaped leaves. A short cluster of greenish flowers appears centrally; red berries develop later near the base and may persist into winter.
Central and southern China and southern Japan; cultivated in shade elsewhere.
Evergreen clump arising from a rhizome, without a tall aerial stem.
Long leathery basal leaves, lanceolate to strap-shaped, with parallel veins.
Short cluster of inconspicuous greenish-white flowers with six perianth parts.
Bright red fleshy berries clustered on a short spike near the rosette centre.
Sun pitcher plant
Heliamphora heterodoxa
tepui pitcher plant
A carnivorous rosette whose leaves form open pitchers that hold water and trap prey. A spoon-shaped nectar appendage rises at the rim. White flowers occur on a separate scape above the pitchers.
Tepuis of south-eastern Venezuela and the Guiana Highlands, in very wet montane scrub.
Rosette of upright pitcher leaves with flared rims and nectar appendages.
Leaves modified into open tubular pitchers with a nectar spoon at the top.
White flowers on a separate aerial scape above the pitchers.
Dry capsule containing numerous fine seeds.
Snow heath
Woollsia pungens
prickly woollsia
A small Australian heath-family shrub with fine branches and narrow alternate leaves ending in a stiff point. Its bell- to urn-shaped flowers are white to pink and axillary.
Endemic to eastern Australia, in heathland and open forest, often on sandy soils.
Low erect shrub with many slender branches.
Leaves alternate, small, narrow and pungent at the tip.
Axillary bell- to urn-shaped flowers, white to pink, with five lobes.
Dry several-celled capsule containing minute seeds.
Tree germander
Teucrium fruticans
shrubby germander

An evergreen Mediterranean shrub with whitish pubescent young shoots. Its small opposite leaves are grey-green above and whitish beneath; pale blue flowers have an almost one-lipped corolla and exserted stamens.
Western and central Mediterranean, in dry scrub and sunny rocky places.
Branched shrub with often arching shoots and white-hairy young wood.
Opposite simple oval leaves, grey-green above and whitish beneath.
Pale blue almost one-lipped flowers with conspicuously exserted stamens.
Four small dry nutlets develop inside the calyx.
Chilean fuchsia-bush
Vestia foetida
huevil
An evergreen Chilean shrub with pale hairy young stems, simple leaves and pendent yellow tubular flowers. The plant and its alkaloids are toxic; animal poisonings are documented. Do not consume.
Endemic to central and southern Chile, in damp scrub and forest margins.
Erect branched evergreen shrub with pubescent young shoots.
Simple opposite elliptic leaves, dark green above and paler beneath.
Pendent yellow tubular flowers with five recurved lobes and exserted stamens.
Dry capsule retained in the calyx; the plant is toxic.
Iboga
Tabernanthe iboga
eboga; iboga

A Central African forest-understorey shrub with opposite leaves and cream flowers marked red-purple. Its root and root bark contain ibogaine; clinical literature reports QT prolongation, potentially fatal arrhythmias and associated deaths. Do not consume or self-medicate.
Central Africa from Cameroon to eastern DR Congo and northern Angola; humid forest understorey.
Branched shrub to about 4 m, with white latex.
Opposite simple entire elliptic to obovate leaves with acuminate tips.
Small regular five-parted cream or white flowers, often marked in the throat.
Smooth pendent globose to ovoid berry, yellow to red, with many seeds.
European boxthorn
Lycium europaeum
Mediterranean boxthorn

A much-branched, often spiny Mediterranean shrub with narrow leaves in small fascicles. Solitary reddish-purple tubular flowers precede small red berries. Berries and spiny habit alone do not distinguish all Lycium species.
Mediterranean region from southern Europe to North Africa and the Levant, in dry scrub and hedges.
A 2–4 m shrub with greyish branches and stout lateral spines.
Narrow lanceolate to oblanceolate entire leaves, often in fascicles.
Usually solitary flowers with a long reddish-purple tube and short lobes.
Small globose red berry; identification also uses leaves, flowers and spines.
Cretanweed
Hedypnois rhagadioloides
Hedypnois

A small annual rosette plant with rough toothed to lobed leaves and yellow ligulate heads. The two involucral bract rows differ and become distinctive in fruit. POWO treats the name as a synonym of Leontodon rhagadioloides, while several regional floras retain Hedypnois.
Mediterranean region and Macaronesia, in dry grassland, disturbed ground and open soils.
Annual with a basal rosette and branched flowering stems, usually low to medium in height.
Rough basal leaves, oblong to oblanceolate, toothed or lobed.
Head of yellow ligulate florets; involucre has two unequal rows of bracts.
Achenes vary by position, sometimes curved and associated with persistent inner bracts.
Takakiaceae
Bryophyte family including Takakia, an unusual moss with deeply lobed leaves.
Takakia family
Polytrichaceae
A family of often robust mosses whose leaves bear photosynthetic lamellae.
Hair-cap mosses
Ricciaceae
Thalloid liverworts whose flattened gametophytes often branch dichotomously.
Crystalworts
